Problem 622. Pairwise collective choice: Library versus Sports Hall
Group preferences can be aggregated in different ways. Pairwise majority asks a specific question about two options at a time.

Three public projects are considered: Park, Library, Sports Hall. Voter groups and rankings: 5 voters rank Park>Library>Sports Hall; 6 voters rank Library>Sports Hall>Park; 3 voters rank Sports Hall>Park>Library. Use pairwise majority: compare two options at a time; each voter supports the one ranked higher.

In a pairwise vote between Library and Sports Hall, which option wins?
1. For each group, check whether Library or Sports Hall is ranked higher. 2. Totals: Library=11, Sports Hall=3. 3. Therefore the result is Library.

Part B — New and mixed reasoning domains
Map scale links a model to the real world through proportional reasoning.
A map has scale 1:10000. The measured map distance between two points is 5 cm. Rule: 1 cm on the map represents 10000 cm in reality; 100,000 cm = 1 km.
Multiply map length by the scale denominator, then convert units. A scale is a ratio, not an added distance.
What is the real straight-line distance in kilometres?
Scale problems are ratio problems: keep units explicit and conversion becomes mechanical.
Proportion d_real=d_map×denominator, followed by unit conversion.

Problem 631. Locating a point by constraints: case 1
Coordinates turn location into numbers. Multiple spatial clues can be treated as simultaneous constraints.
A point P lies on an integer grid with x,y from 0 to 7. It satisfies x+y=6 and x−y=0. It also satisfies x≥2.
A location is valid only if it satisfies every stated equation and inequality at the same time.
Which coordinate(s) can P occupy? Is the solution unique?
1. List pairs satisfying x+y=6. 2. Keep only those also satisfying x−y=0. 3. The remaining set is [(3, 3)].
A constraint problem is solved by satisfying all conditions together, not one at a time independently.
